content: Thioacetazone, also known by various names such as thiocetazone, thiacetazone, thiosemicarbazone, benzothiozane, or amithiozone, is an anti-tuberculosis medication. It is abbreviated as T. This drug is utilized in the treatment of tuberculosis, but it exhibits only weak activity against Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Its primary role is to prevent the development of resistance to more potent anti-tuberculosis drugs, such as isoniazid and rifampicin. Thioacetazone is never administered as a standalone treatment for tuberculosis. Instead, it is used in combination with other drugs, in a manner similar to ethambutol. However, unlike other anti-tuberculosis medications, thioacetazone is ineffective when administered intermittently. If a treatment regimen already includes ethambutol, there is no additional benefit to incorporating thioacetazone. Despite this, many countries in sub-Saharan Africa continue to use thioacetazone due to its extremely low cost. The use of thioacetazone is decreasing globally because it is associated with severe, and sometimes fatal, skin reactions, particularly in patients who are HIV-positive.
